 B.C. Conservatives projected to win 1st majority in nearly a century after Eby's election gamble backfires | CBC Loaded LIVE UPDATES BRITISH COLUMBIA VOTES B.C. Conservatives projected to win 1st majority in nearly a century after Eby's election gamble backfires
 Updated 8 minutes ago Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says province is 'definitely blue' as Eby resigns NDP leadership CBC News projects a B.C. Conservative majority government
 2 hours ago | Duration closed caption 1:59 CBC News is projecting the B.C. Conservative Party, led by the 'accidental leader' Lorne Doerkson, will win the majority of seats in the province's legislature. The Latest
 The B.C. Conservatives have toppled the incumbent B.C. NDP to win a majority government, CBC News projects, the party's first since 1928.
 "B.C. is definitely blue," Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson said in a jubilant victory speech.
 David Eby, who called an election two years early in hopes his party would win a stronger, fourth term, resigned as premier and NDP leader in his concession speech. 
 Green Party Leader Emily Lowan is projected to win her first seat in the legislature, while the leaders of OneBC and CentreBC are both projected to lose their seats.
 CBC News has live election night coverage on this page, as well as in the video above. For riding-by-riding results, tap here .

 8 minutes ago Some NDP cabinet ministers lose seats
 Lauren Vanderdeen Jodie Wickens, who was minister of children and family development, with David Eby during a campaign stop in Coquitlam, B.C., on Thursday. (Rich Lam/The Canadian Press) Six members of the NDP cabinet are projected to lose their seats at this point:
 Jagrup Brar in Surrey-Fleetwood, who was minister of mining and critical minerals
 Jessie Sunner in Surrey Newton, who was former minister of post-secondary education and future skills
 Rick Glumac in Port Moody-Burquitlam, who was minister of state for artificial intelligence and new technologies
 Jodie Wickens in Coquitlam-Burke Mountain, who was minister of children and family development.
 Anne Kang in Burnaby Centre, who was minister of tourism, arts and sport 
 Terry Yung in Vancouver-Yaletown, who was minister of state for community safety and integrated services
 There are still two races in which cabinet ministers are running that CBC News has not yet projected; 15 former cabinet ministers have kept their seats.
 Some cabinet ministers decided not to run in this snap election, including former health minister Ravi Kahlon, former minister of emergency management Kelly Greene, and former agriculture minister Lana Popham.
 Copy the link to this update: Some NDP cabinet ministers lose seats 
 27 minutes ago Eby has lost the election. What is his legacy?
 Justin McElroy Eby during his resignation speech. (Jennifer Gauthier/Reuters) David Eby’s four years as premier of British Columbia have come to a close, and he has resigned as leader of the B.C. NDP as the party looks set for its worst election result in 25 years.  
 Eby was heralded as an effective opposition critic against the B.C. Liberals on the housing and money laundering files. As attorney general, he led a number of tough files, including ICBC reform and the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA), and did well enough that no one from the party establishment challenged him for the leadership when John Horgan retired.
 But being an effective premier is different than being an effective cabinet minister. Eby's reign as leader was marked by decreasing rental rates and a focus on building more housing, but also escalating deficits and a series of backtracks: on drug decriminalization, on the carbon tax, and on  attempts to change DRIPA. The Conservatives centred their campaign around people’s lack of enthusiasm for Eby, and it worked in spades. 
 The passage of time often rehabilitates the reputations of past leaders — but in the immediate aftermath of a disastrous election, Eby’s legacy is decidedly mixed. 
 Copy the link to this update: Eby has lost the election. What is his legacy? 
 38 minutes ago In midst of loss, Eby still projected to win seat
 Lauren Vanderdeen Eby tonight. (Jennifer Gauthier/Reuters) Eby is projected to win his seat in the Vancouver-Point Grey riding, despite losing the premiership.
 Eby was first elected as the MLA for Vancouver–Point Grey in 2013, defeating then-premier Christy Clark. He was re-elected in 2017, 2020 and 2024, securing a fourth term as MLA. 
 Copy the link to this update: In midst of loss, Eby still projected to win seat 
 39 minutes ago Green Party leader celebrates winning seat, braces for Conservative majority
 Emily Fagan FULL SPEECH: Green Party Leader Emily Lowan speaks after party wins 2 seats
 18 minutes ago | Duration closed caption 19:27 Green Party Leader Emily Lowan spoke to party supporters after winning her own seat along with re-elected West Vancouver-Sea to Sky MLA Jeremy Valeriote. She said they 'may have a small caucus but we have inherited an enormous responsibility,' and promised to hold the incoming Conservative government accountable.
 Lowan has taken the stage amid a shower of confetti to address a room of supporters celebrating the party holding two seats in the legislature. Lowan has been projected to win the Vancouver Island riding of Saanich North and the Islands.
 She says that over the next four years her job is to be a voice for those she believes will be harmed by a B.C. Conservative government.
 "We may have a small caucus, but tonight we have inherited an enormous responsibility, and that is to hold a majority Conservative government to account," she says.
 "We're holding the weight of the joy of this victory, and what comes tomorrow."
 She says her party will stand with and fight for those impacted by anticipated cuts and attacks on human rights. 
 Copy the link to this update: Green Party leader celebrates winning seat, braces for Conservative majority 
 46 minutes ago Tight races in some ridings
 Maryse Zeidler and Brady Strachan B.C. Green Party supporters watching results from Brentwood Bay, B.C., tonight. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press) While CBC News has projected a Conservative majority, there are still some tight races throughout the province. 
 At the watch party for Conservative incumbent Brennan Day for Courtenay-Comox, the mood is mixed. On the one hand people are feeling good about the Conservative win, but they're also hesitant. It's been a tight race all night, just like it was two years ago. But in the past hour, the NDP's Will Cole-Hamilton has taken the lead.
 CBC News spoke with Day earlier, and he said it's been a long couple of months for him. He went into this campaign as an Independent after he briefly left the party caucus under Kerry-Lynne Findlay's leadership.
 Meanwhile in the Interior, the Kelowna Centre riding remains a close race and the lead has changed hands through the night from the NDP’s Loyal Wooldridge to incumbent Kristina Loewen for the Conservatives. 
 Conservative supporters have been cheering loudly as they’ve watched Loewen increase her lead as results continue to come in. 
 If she succeeds, it will be a map of blue across the Okanagan.
 Copy the link to this update: Tight races in some ridings 
 59 minutes ago Doerkson ends his speech with a rallying cry
 Lauren Vanderdeen Doerkson on stage. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press) Doerkson shared a message to First Nations.
 "This future is one we will build together as partners with the certainty all of us needs," Doerkson said.
 His party campaigned on repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, which was unanimously passed in 2019. It's the province's framework for reconciliation, but the Conservatives said it has created "unnecessary uncertainty."
 "I am going to give this job everything that I have got, I promise you that,"  Doerkson says.
 "And I also promise you that I won't get it all perfect. But when I don't, I'm going to tell you and then I will get back to work."
 He says he wants to shake every hand in the room tonight.
 Copy the link to this update: Doerkson ends his speech with a rallying cry 
 1 hour ago Doerkson outlines future of Conservative majority
 Lauren Vanderdeen Doerkson during tonight's speech. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press) Doerkson is making promises in his victory speech. He says Vancouver will host a business summit next year that will be the "envy of the world."
 "We will welcome capital back to our province," Doerkson says.
 He promises to double natural gas production by 2032 and triple it by 2035. He wants to cut red tape "like never before."
 "We will be the catalyst, I promise you that. But you are the engine."
 And another pledge: a $1,000 tax cut and no new taxes. 
 Copy the link to this update: Doerkson outlines future of Conservative majority 
 1 hour ago Doerkson full of joy in victory speech
 Lauren Vanderdeen Doerkson arrives for his victory speech. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press) Lorne Doerkson has walked out to Fleetwood Mac's Don't Stop for his victory speech. He entered Conservative headquarters to sparklers, celebrations and jubilant hugs.
 "B.C. is definitely blue," yells Doerkson.
 He's thanking candidates, supporters and all voters. Doerkson, who has been repeatedly described as mild-mannered during this campaign, is full of energy and excitement. This is not a mild-mannered speech.
 "I have had a lot of coffee in the last couple of weeks. Frankly, I've had quite a bit tonight," he said. 
 He promised he will work as hard as the volunteers worked on the campaign — and he's promising to "supercharge British Columbia."
 He says it won't happen on one street or one city, but all over.
 "A mill running in Quesnel keeps a trucker working in Surrey. A mine opening in the north keeps a port busy in Delta. It's one economy and it runs through every town on our map in British Columbia."
 Copy the link to this update: Doerkson full of joy in victory speech 
 2 hours ago Emily Lowan projected to win 1st seat as MLA
 Lauren Vanderdeen Lowan, right, hugs a friend tonight. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press) CBC News is projecting B.C. Green Party Leader Emily Lowan will be the next MLA for Saanich North and the Islands.
 Elected as party leader last year, Lowan did not have a seat in the legislature. In her first campaign for public office, she ran in the riding formerly held by the Greens' Rob Botterell.
 Lowan, 26, has previously worked as a climate activist and a policy researcher.
 Copy the link to this update: Emily Lowan projected to win 1st seat as MLA 
 2 hours ago Eby resigns as premier, B.C. NDP leader as he concedes election
 Tara Carman FULL SPEECH: David Eby concedes and resigns as NDP leader
 1 hour ago | Duration closed caption 6:11 David Eby, speaking to party supporters, has conceded the election and resigned as NDP leader. He says he spoke to the Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson and wished him the best as the incoming premier of British Columbia.
 Eby is giving his concession speech at a downtown Vancouver hotel. He says he congratulated Doerkson on winning a majority government.
 “The people of British Columbia have asked us to be the Official Opposition," Eby said.
 “It breaks my heart and I accept full responsibility for that outcome.”
 He then offered his resignation as premier and B.C. NDP leader. Eby he’s looking forward to spending more time with his wife and three young children.
 “My family has paid a very significant cost for this work," he said.
 He ended his speech by telling his wife, Dr. Cailey Lynch, that he loves her and saying, “let’s go home."
